Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On Sat, 17 Jan 2004 03:37:40 -0800, Kevin M. wrote:

>We should probably ban Succubus Club right away

>...

>Just be honest with yourself and say that you're against players talking
>during the game.

Succubus Club specifically allows players to make deals. Malkavian
Game does not. These cards tell you how they should be played.
Subverting the stated function of the card is wrong. Computer gamers
have the useful term "exploit" for this kind of thing. In multiplayer
games, use of exploits is usually considered to be cheating. And so
it is here. Players who collude to rig a Malkavian Game are cheats.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Eric Simon
Messages.Body:
"Orpheus" <orph...@DEADSPAMfree.fr> wrote in message news:<40092323$0$1161$636a...@news.free.fr>...

> 2) I don't see where "talking" during the game is involved with the
> Malkavian Prank (the one where plain pre-planned cheating can be involved) ;
> as with the Malkavian Game, the move is obvious to all, so I just have to
> know if it's legal or not

In both cases it's not collusion, it's *table management*. When your
grandprey is low on pool, or you make a cross-table deal, why in the
world wouldn't it be legal to tell someone as you play the Malkavian
Prank, "I will choose 1 for you" (meaning they can gain 4)?
Similarly, why wouldn't you be able to tell someone "I'm feeling
rocky" when you play Malkavian Game if you think they need pool? The
problem that I have with banning individual cards for collusion is
that this game is more complicated than that. It might be collusion
when I oust myself with MG without having gained a VP. But it might
be table-management if I'm using it to keep my grand-prey from being
ousted to set up the sweep.

> 3) I ask this because a player who tries to find loopholes in the game asked
> me these very same questions. It is my duty as judge and organiser to be
> able to give him correct answers. I have no personnal feeling involved in
> these questions.

Again, I'm not sure that I consider this a loophole. My Malkavian
"Let's Play Games" deck was designed to intentionally upset table
balance and then manually reset it to a balance of my choosing. I did
that through combinations of Game of Malkav, Malkavian Game, Malkavian
Prank and Petra Resonance (and lots of Kindred Spirits). Sometimes,
the MG and MP were used specifically to help people cross-table,
sometimes not. It depends on the levels of pool at the table.

Personally, what I think it comes down to is that collusion is a
behavior that is independent of cards. Nearly every tournament-viable
deck *could* be built for collusion, because the key to winning this
game is table management. So the task of the judge is simply to look
for behavior in which a player is not trying to max VP.

Eric Simon
Prince of Chicago

It explicitly allows players to make trades.

The fact that it doesn't restrict their inherent ability to make deals
in no way means that that ability wasn't there already.

> Game does not. These cards tell you how they should be played.

Malkavian Game does not restrict a player's ability to make (and break)
deals.

Malkavian Game sets up a forced trade (the terms of which are decided
by a specified series of RPS games). Succubus Club allows a trade to
be set up (but the trade is not forced and the terms of the trade are
a bit more free-form).

> have the useful term "exploit" for this kind of thing. In multiplayer
> games, use of exploits is usually considered to be cheating. And so
> it is here. Players who collude to rig a Malkavian Game are cheats.

Exploiting the +1 stealth from Bonding is not cheating.
Exploiting the effects of a card is not cheating.

On Mon, 19 Jan 2004 08:08:37 -0500, LSJ wrote:

>The fact that it doesn't restrict their inherent ability to make deals
>in no way means that that ability wasn't there already.

I've looked through the latest rules in Black Hand and they don't seem
to say anything about this. There is no provision for deal-making in
the sequence of play, the glossary, the index, or the examples of
play. So far as one can tell from that rulebook, this is not a game
of deal making and breaking. That's no change - the rules have never
permitted such things.

I've been playing an online computer game lately (Hearts of Iron,
which I recommend). I was amused at the weekend, when a US player
complained that the other players didn't write good English. I
observed that I was the only English player in the game - the others
were French, Spanish, Finnish, etc. He, as an American, barely
qualified :). I have a smattering of German and French but am soon
left behind when other players converse in such languages, let alone
Finnish (which looks like line noise).

The official pretext for banning Madness of the Bard was that it was
unfair to players who were not fluent in the local language. How much
worse it must be for such players when unlimited deal-making is added
to the game. I am amazed that it is tolerated at the top-tier Euro
events which attract such a polyglot crowd. I'd have thought that
only parochial Americans could suppose that everyone should be able to
speak good English ...

Andrew

Messages.Author: LSJ

Andrew S. Davidson wrote:
> The rulebook does still cite the
> newsgroup while it still makes no mention of deals. Thank you.

As we've been over before, it makes no mention of things like breathing
or talking, yes.

Deals (making, breaking) are not restricted. Breathing (in, out) is
not restricted.

The rules and card texts tell you what you can do with your cards (how
the decks are constructed, how and when they can be played and what
effect they have when played) and counters (where they start and how they
move and what effects they have) and the edge (where it starts and how
it moves and what effects it has) etc. (game state stuff).

Deals, breathing, and other things that do not affect the game state are
not described in the rules, since the purpose of the game rules is to
describe the game state and the things that affect game state.

>Deals, breathing, and other things that do not affect the game state are

So, we agree that deals are not a formal part of the game. They are
like breathing - an extraneous factor. The difference is that
breathing is an involuntary action which the players must perform to
stay alive but which does not usually disrupt the game. This is not
true of deal-making. Players are trying to make this part of the game
when it is not. It's as inappropriate as wrestling, sleight of hand
or other trickery. These may assist the player in some manner but, as
these actions are not part of the game, they should not be allowed to
interfere with it.

Andrew

Messages.Author: Daneel

> > So, we agree that deals are not a formal part of the game. They are
> > like breathing - an extraneous factor. The difference is that
> > breathing is an involuntary action which the players must perform to
> > stay alive but which does not usually disrupt the game. This is not

>
> Yes, it is, as far as that goes.
> Deal making has no impact on the game.
> That is, it doesn't affect the game state at all.
> The game state before and after deals is still altered only in ways
> allowed by the rules and card text.

That is only partly true.

The general tournament rules (and specifically those regarding
sportsmanship) state clearly that one needs to intend to Win /
maximize VPs. In this sense it is a rule.

A legally made deal (that is, one that maximizes my VPs _from the
point it is made at_) will impact the legal status, because it will
allow me to (for example) root the "maximize VPs" clause back to the
point of the deal. This is essential to honor losing (and sometimes
even winning) deals. Otherwise the rules would force the player to
break his word, once through a losing deal he achieved the (otherwise
unattainable) 2 VPs and it would be time for him to lay down to the
winning player.

Best Regards,

Daneel
